name: Vienna Game
tagline: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 – a quick, attacking White opening where f2-f4 opens the f-file and you play for the initiative from move 3.
ideas: **Nc3 before Nf3** keeps the f-pawn free, so you can play **f2-f4** and open the f-file for your rook.
Against 2...Nf6 the **Vienna Gambit 3.f4** is the main weapon: after 3...d5 4.fxe5 your pawn on e5 kicks the f6 knight and gains space.
If Black takes 3...exf4, push **4.e5** and then **Nf3** – the knight on f3 stops ...Qh4+ and you win the f4 pawn back later with Bxf4.
With Bc4 lines, remember the **fork trick** ...Nxe4 (Nxe4 d5): play d3 early when you want a calm game.
Typical attack: castle short, rook on f1 behind the f-pawn, queen to e1-g3 or f3, and push f4-f5 against Black's king.

lines.name: Vienna Gambit: 3.f4 d5 (main line)
lines.intro: This is the most important Vienna line. After 2...Nf6 you play 3.f4, and the best reply 3...d5 leads to an open fight where your e5 pawn gives you space.

moves.text: The king's pawn takes the center (d5 and f5) and opens lines for your queen and light-squared bishop.
Black copies you: the pawn grabs its share of the center and stops you from playing d4 for free.
The **Vienna move**. The knight develops, defends e4 and watches d5. Notice it does NOT block the f-pawn, unlike Nf3 – you want to play f4 soon.
Black develops and attacks the e4 pawn. It is defended by your knight, so there is no danger.
The **Vienna Gambit**. You attack e5 and want to open the f-file. If Black takes on f4, your plan is e4-e5 to kick the f6 knight.
Black's best answer: hit back in the center instead of grabbing the pawn. Black wants to open lines while your king is still in the middle.
Take the pawn. Now your pawn on e5 attacks the knight on f6, so Black has to react immediately.
The knight jumps to a strong central square and attacks your c3 knight. It is supported by the d5 pawn.
Develop and protect the e5 pawn. You also prepare d4 to build a big center. 5.Qf3 is another good option, but Nf3 is the most natural.
Black develops calmly and prepares to castle.
Now you have pawns on d4 and e5 – lots of space. The c1 bishop can also come out.
Black puts the king in safety before opening more lines.
The bishop develops to an active square: it attacks the e4 knight and aims at h7, close to Black's king.
Black supports the strong e4 knight with a pawn so it cannot easily be traded or chased away.
**En passant!** Black's f-pawn moved two squares past your e5 pawn, so you can capture it as if it had moved one square. This removes the support of the e4 knight and opens the f-file.
Black recaptures with the bishop, which now points at your d4 pawn.
Castle! Your king is safe and your rook stands on the half-open f-file.
Black develops and adds a second attacker to d4 (knight + bishop).
Trade off Black's best piece, the centralized knight.
Black recaptures. The new e4 pawn attacks BOTH your bishop on d3 and your knight on f3 – a pawn fork.
Solve the fork by simply taking the pawn. You are now a pawn up, but your d4 pawn is attacked twice.

lines.summary: The position is open and about equal. Watch your d4 pawn: Black will probably win it back with ...Nxd4, so continue developing with Be3 or c3 and use the open f-file for your rooks.

lines.name: Vienna Gambit: 3...exf4 4.e5
lines.intro: Many players at your level grab the pawn with 3...exf4. Here you show why that gives you a fast, comfortable game.

moves.text: Take the center and open lines for the queen and bishop.
Black takes an equal share of the center.
Develop, defend e4, and keep the f-pawn free to advance.
Black develops and puts pressure on e4.
The Vienna Gambit: offer a pawn to open the f-file and gain time.
Black accepts the pawn. It is not a blunder, but it lets you gain a lot of time against the f6 knight.
Kick the knight! It has no good central square: d5 and e4 are covered, so it usually has to go back home.
The safest retreat. Black has now moved the same knight twice and is back where it started – you are ahead in development.
Very important move: the knight stops **...Qh4+**, which would be annoying with the f-pawn gone. It also develops and supports e5.
Black attacks your e5 pawn to open lines and free the position.
Support e5 and open the c1 bishop's path to f4, where Black's extra pawn lives.
Black takes on e5, hoping to keep the extra pawn.
Your queen now looks down the e-file at Black's king. You will recapture on e5 with check.
Black develops with a pin: the bishop attacks c3, and the knight is pinned to your king.
Take back the pawn with check. Black must deal with the check before doing anything else.
Black blocks and offers a queen trade.
You win back the second pawn as well. Material is equal and your pieces are much more active.

lines.summary: Material is equal, but you have more pieces developed and Black's king is still in the center. A queen trade on e5 is fine for you – just finish development with Bd3 and O-O-O or O-O.

lines.name: 3.Bc4 Nxe4: the Frankenstein-Dracula (danger!)
lines.intro: If you play 3.Bc4 instead of 3.f4, Black can answer 3...Nxe4!. This leads to the famous wild Frankenstein-Dracula line, where you win a rook but your queen and knight can get into big trouble. Know it, or simply play 3.f4 against 2...Nf6.

moves.text: Take the center.
Black takes the center too.
The Vienna knight: develops and defends e4, keeps f-pawn free.
Black develops and attacks e4.
Develop the bishop toward f7, the weakest point in Black's camp.
The **fork trick**: Black takes the pawn. If 4.Nxe4, then ...d5 forks your bishop and knight and Black gets the piece back.
The sharpest answer: you threaten **Qxf7#** (the bishop on c4 supports the queen).
The only good defense: the knight defends f7 and attacks your bishop at the same time.
Keep the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal so it still points at f7.
This starts the **Frankenstein-Dracula**. Black develops and is ready to give up a rook for a dangerous attack. (5...Be7 is the calmer choice.)
Attack the d6 knight (the defender of f7) and threaten Nxc7+, forking king and rook.
Black attacks your queen to gain time.
The queen comes back with a new threat: Qxf7# down the f-file.
Black blocks the f-file with a pawn.
Threatening mate on f7 a third time, now along the diagonal with the bishop behind the queen.
The queen defends f7. Black is now ready to let you take the rook.
Fork! Check to the king and attack on the a8 rook.
The king steps aside; it is the only move.
You win a whole rook. But look: your knight on a8 is now stuck in the corner.
Black traps the knight (it cannot escape from a8) and opens b7 for the bishop, which will attack your queen and the long diagonal toward your king.

lines.summary: You are a rook up, but your knight on a8 is trapped and Black gets a big attack with ...Bb7 and ...Nd4. Experts say it is roughly balanced, but it is very easy to lose as White. Beginners should prefer 3.f4 against 2...Nf6.

lines.name: 3.Bc4 Bc5: the calm copycat
lines.intro: When Black copies you with 3...Bc5, protect e4 with d3 and then play the Vienna's favorite move f4.

moves.text: Take the center.
Black takes the center too.
Develop, defend e4 and keep the f-pawn free.
Black develops and attacks e4.
Develop the bishop toward f7.
Black copies you. The bishop aims at your f2 square and also supports a later ...Nxe4 trick.
Protect e4 firmly so the fork trick does not work, and open the c1 bishop.
Black does the same: e5 is protected and the c8 bishop can come out.
The Vienna plan. You attack e5 and prepare to open the f-file. Careful: with Black's bishop on c5 you cannot castle short until that diagonal is blocked or the bishop is traded.
Black adds a second defender to e5.
Develop and add pressure on e5. You are almost ready to castle.
Black gives the c5 bishop a safe retreat square (a7) so that Na4 cannot trade it off.
Grab space on the kingside. The pawn on f5 blocks Black's c8 bishop and prepares g4-g5 to attack the f6 knight.
Black stops Bg5, which would pin the f6 knight.
Connect your pieces and prepare Be3 to challenge Black's strong c5 bishop. Castling long is also possible later.

lines.summary: Equal but rich position. Your plan is Be3 to trade Black's best bishop, then g4-g5 to attack. Black wants ...Na5 to trade your c4 bishop, or ...d5 in the center.

lines.name: 2...Nc6: Bc4, d3 and f4
lines.intro: Against 2...Nc6 the simplest plan is Bc4, d3, f4 and Nf3. You keep the game calm but still attack on the kingside.

moves.text: Take the center.
Black takes the center too.
Develop, defend e4 and keep the f-pawn free.
Black develops the queen's knight and defends e5.
Develop the bishop to its best diagonal, aiming at f7.
Black develops and attacks e4.
Defend e4 calmly. Now ...Nxe4 tricks do not work and your c1 bishop can develop.
Black develops the bishop to its most active square, aiming at f2.
Vienna style: hit e5 and get ready to open the f-file.
Black supports e5 without giving up the center.
Develop and attack e5 again. If Black plays 6...Ng4 to hit f2, calmly defend with Qe2 – the knight on g4 achieves nothing.
Black castles short. Now you know where the king lives, and you can aim your pawns at it.

Black puts the knight on a strong central square.
Trade off this strong knight before it becomes annoying.
Black recaptures with the bishop.
Bring the queen toward the kingside, ready for g4-g5.
Black prepares ...d5 or ...b5 to counter in the center and on the queenside.
Move the bishop away early so that ...d5 or ...b5 does not hit it with tempo.

lines.summary: A good attacking setup for you: plan g4-g5, Ne2 (to kick the d4 bishop with c3), and h4. Black will try ...d5 to break in the center, so keep an eye on e4.

lines.name: Trap: 3...Nxe4 4.Qh5 Nf6?? 5.Qxf7#
lines.intro: After 3.Bc4 Nxe4 4.Qh5, Black MUST play 4...Nd6. If Black retreats with the 'natural' 4...Nf6??, it is mate in one.

moves.text: Take the center.
Black takes the center too.
The Vienna knight develops.
Black develops and attacks e4.
The bishop aims at f7.
Black takes the pawn with the fork trick idea.
Threatening Qxf7# with the bishop's support. Also the queen attacks the e5 pawn.
A blunder! The knight attacks your queen, but it does not defend f7. (4...Nd6 was the only move.)
Checkmate! The bishop on c4 protects the queen, so the king cannot take, and all its escape squares are covered.

lines.summary: Always look for checks and captures on f7 when your queen and bishop both aim there. If Black plays 4...Nd6 correctly, continue with 5.Bb3.

name: Italian Game
tagline: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 – the classic way to learn open games: fast development, the f7 target and a slow, safe c3-d3 plan.
ideas: **Bc4 aims at f7**, the square only Black's king defends at the start.
The modern plan is the **Giuoco Pianissimo**: c3, d3, O-O, Re1, a4/Bb3 and the knight tour **Nbd2-f1-g3**.
**c3 prepares d4** – if you get pawns on d4 and e4, you control the center.
Against 3...Nf6 you can try **4.Ng5** (attacking f7 twice), but know that 5...Na5! is Black's correct defense.
Play **h3** in time to stop ...Bg4 and ...Ng4, which pin or attack your king's side.

lines.name: Giuoco Pianissimo: c3, d3 and the Nbd2-f1-g3 plan
lines.intro: The slow, solid main line that strong players use today. You build a safe position first and attack later.

moves.text: Take the center and open lines for the queen and the f1 bishop.
Black takes the center too.
Develop with a threat: the knight attacks the e5 pawn.
Black develops and defends e5 at the same time – the most natural move.
The **Italian bishop**. It controls d5 and aims at f7, Black's weakest square.
The **Giuoco Piano** ('quiet game'). Black's bishop copies yours and aims at f2.
Prepares d4 to build a big center, and gives your bishop a retreat square on c2 later.
Black develops and attacks e4.
The **Pianissimo** ('very quiet'). You protect e4 calmly instead of opening the game. You keep d3-d4 for later.
Black protects e5 and frees the c8 bishop.
Castle: your king is safe behind its pawns and the rook is ready to come to the center.
Black castles short, putting the king in safety and bringing the rook closer to the center.

Black prepares ...Ba7 so the bishop is safe from d4 or b4 pawn attacks.
Move the bishop before Black can hit it with ...Na5 or ...b5. On b3 it still aims at f7.
Black tucks the bishop away on a7, where no pawn can attack it.
Start the famous **knight tour**: d2, f1, then g3, where the knight helps the kingside attack.
Black offers to trade your strong b3 bishop. If you take on e6, Black's f-pawn recaptures and the f-file opens for Black, so usually do not take.

Black supports e5 and prepares ...d5 one day.
Stop ...Ng4 and ...Bg4. Your king also gets a safe escape square.

lines.summary: A calm, equal position with many pieces. Your plans: d3-d4 in the center, Be3 to trade Black's a7 bishop, Nh4-f5 on the kingside. Black's main break is ...d5.

lines.name: Giuoco Piano: c3 and d4 (open center)
lines.intro: The older, sharper way: you play d4 at once to take the center. Black must strike back with ...d5 at the right moment.

Black makes d5 rock-solid.

lines.name: Two Knights: 4.Ng5 and the Fried Liver Attack
lines.intro: After 3...Nf6 you can attack f7 with 4.Ng5. If Black answers 5...Nxd5? you can sacrifice a knight on f7 – the famous Fried Liver Attack.

Black takes the center too.
Develop and attack e5.
Develop and defend e5.
Aim at f7.

Take the pawn. Now the bishop and the d5 pawn both look toward Black's position.

Black wins a knight, but the king is pulled out into the open.

Black defends d5 again and threatens ...Nxc2+, forking your king and rook.

Open more lines toward Black's king and free your c1 bishop.

lines.intro: Good players answer 4.Ng5 with 5...Na5!, sacrificing a pawn for fast development. You must know how to keep your extra pawn safely.

Move the bishop with check so Black has to answer you first.
Black blocks and attacks the bishop and the d5 pawn.

Your bishop on a3 stops Black from castling short, because the king would have to cross f8.

lines.name: Trap: Legal's Mate
lines.intro: A 250-year-old trap. If Black pins your f3 knight early and plays slowly, you can 'give away' your queen and checkmate.

moves.text: Take the center.
Black takes the center too.
Develop and attack e5.
The Philidor Defense: Black protects e5 with a pawn.
Aim at f7.
Black pins your knight to your queen – if the knight moves, the queen can be taken.
Develop. Now e4 is defended and the knight can later jump to d5.
A slow mistake. Black ignores the danger on f7.
Ignore the pin! You 'hang' your queen, but if Black takes it, it is mate. If Black plays 5...dxe5 instead, then 6.Qxg4 and you simply won a pawn.
Black greedily takes the queen.

The only move.
**Legal's Mate**: three minor pieces checkmate the king. Every escape square is covered.

lines.summary: The lesson: a pin to the queen is not absolute – the pinned piece can still move if it creates a bigger threat. Always check what happens if your opponent takes the 'free' queen.

name: Caro-Kann Defense
tagline: 1.e4 c6 – a rock-solid answer to 1.e4: you support ...d5 with the c-pawn and get your light-squared bishop out before ...e6.
ideas: **...c6 then ...d5**: you challenge e4 with a pawn that is always protected.
Get the **light-squared bishop out (...Bf5 or ...Bg4) BEFORE playing ...e6** – this is the Caro-Kann's big advantage over the French.
Your pawn structure is very healthy, so **endgames are usually good for you**. Trading pieces is not scary.
Typical breaks: **...c5** against the Advance, **...e5** or **...c5** in the Classical.
Danger squares: watch for **Nd6#** and **Bxf7/Ne5** tricks when your knights block each other on d7 and f6.

lines.intro: The most important line. You take on e4, develop the bishop to f5 with tempo, and build a solid position.
